doc.title: Chazz Frichtel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 13, 2016

title: Parents' reaction to the move and the Raquel Welch gig
summary: His mother supported the move, his father was apprehensive until the Lake Tahoe job with Raquel Welch won him over.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did your parents think — what did your parents think of you moving to the other coast?

My mom was all for it. She was the musician in the family and she knew that I had a real passion for it and fortunately she passed her talent on to me. And I think my dad was a little apprehensive. You know, he was a GE engineer guy. And when I first got to L.A. the first year was pretty tough going. I mean some not so fun things happened the first year I was there. But all of that eventually led to kind of my first break, which was two weeks — it was either a week or two weeks in Lake Tahoe with Racquel Welch. And my dad actually flew out to see that show, I wonder why. I’m not so sure it was to see me. But I think at that point he kind of breathed a sigh of relief and I think he became kind of one of my biggest fans and supporters.
He told me before he passed, he said, “I really admire your bravery and your stick-to-it- iveness” if there is such a word.
Were you nervous on that first gig with her? Do you remember?

I don’t know — if I was nervous it was more excitement. Her act was more of a cabaret kind of act. But it was kind of one of my first encounters with celebrity and of course I couldn’t look at her without seeing the 2000 B.C. poster that a lot of us had. But she was very nice and she made me feel welcome and at ease and she was really fun to work with.
It’s funny you say that because Aretha Franklin played here once and I got to play in the horn section.
And we couldn’t afford to like watch her because if you started watching her you’d forget to play. And the conductor’s doing all these things and it’s just like how do you tune out Aretha Franklin?
Yeah. No that was great, and I think that sort of put my dad’s apprehension aside.
